# After Stalin: The Soviet Union and the Eastern Bloc (1953–1968)

## A New Leader

Joseph Stalin died in 1953. Georgy Malenkov briefly took his place as leader of the Soviet Union. Then Nikita Khrushchev became the new leader.

Khrushchev was a strong opponent of the Western Bloc, just like Stalin had been. At one meeting, he bragged that communism would "bury" capitalism. But he also wanted a new attitude toward the United States. He wanted to point the Soviet Union in a new direction.

## De-Stalinization

In February 1956, Khrushchev spoke at the Twentieth Congress of the Soviet Communist Party. He denounced Stalin. He accused Stalin of crimes against the Soviet people.

After that speech, Khrushchev began an aggressive process called de-Stalinization. He changed many policies from the Stalin era:

- He ended censorship of the arts.
- He released many people whom Stalin had jailed for political reasons.
- He dissolved the special tribunals that had convicted them.
- He removed Stalin's name from public buildings.
- He took down monuments to Stalin.

## Poland, 1956

In the Eastern Bloc countries, these changes signaled a political thaw.

In June 1956, workers in Poznan, Poland, rioted. They protested food shortages and poor housing. They also had other grievances. In autumn, protests spread to other Polish cities. The protests had a nationalistic character. Protesters called for the Soviet army to leave Poland. They also wanted Russian language classes removed from Polish school curricula.

In October, Władysław Gomułka became leader of the Polish Communist Party. He was now the leader of Poland. Gomułka called for governmental reforms.

Khrushchev was alarmed. He feared that reforms might pull Poland out of the Eastern Bloc. He mobilized Soviet troops in Poland and marched them toward Warsaw. At the same time, he flew to Poland in person.

Gomułka assured Khrushchev that he had no intention of ending communism. He also said Poland would keep its relationship with the Soviet Union. Khrushchev then agreed that reforms could take place.

The following changes were made:

- The collectivization of Polish agriculture was ended.
- Soviet advisers were sent home.
- Political prisoners were released.
- The Roman Catholic Church was given greater freedom.

## Hungary, 1956

The success in Poland inspired others. On October 23, 1956, students marched through the streets of Budapest, Hungary. They demanded several things:

- Removal of Stalinist symbols.
- Improvements in wages.
- Economic reforms.
- Removal of Soviet troops from Hungary.

The State Security Police opened fire on students who gathered outside the main radio station. The students wanted to read their demands on the air. Several students were killed.

An uprising began. Angry citizens fought both the police and Soviet troops. Protesters attacked the parliament building. Ernő Gerő, head of the ruling Hungarian Working People's Party and leader of the country, fled. His prime minister, András Hegedüs, fled with him.

Imre Nagy took office as prime minister. Nagy was a reformer. Unlike Gomułka, Nagy did not want to make internal reforms while staying loyal to Moscow. He wanted more.

On October 28, Nagy called for a cease-fire. He dissolved the State Security Police. He demanded that Soviet troops leave Budapest. On November 1, he announced that Hungary was no longer a member of the Warsaw Pact. He said Hungary would remain neutral in international affairs.

## The Soviet Invasion of Hungary

Three days later, Soviet forces entered Hungary. They joined troops that the USSR had been about to withdraw until Nagy's announcement.

Why did Khrushchev order the invasion? There are several possible reasons:

- He may have feared that Hungarian neutrality threatened Soviet security.
- He may have wanted to show his resolve to conservative communists and leaders of other Soviet states.
- Some argue that the Western Bloc's failure to intervene emboldened him.

The uprising ended on November 10. About 2,500 Hungarians had been killed. The communist government was reestablished under János Kádár.

Approximately twenty thousand Hungarians were arrested. Another 200,000 fled the country. Soviet troops were permanently stationed in Hungary. In 1958, Nagy was tried and executed.

The United States did not become involved in the events in Hungary. Khrushchev later mocked this decision.

## The Berlin Crisis

Despite not wanting a confrontation with the Soviets, the United States could not ignore Khrushchev's ultimatum regarding Berlin. In 1958 and again in 1961, Khrushchev demanded that Britain, France, and the United States leave West Berlin. These demands went unheeded.

The capitalist part of the old German capital was a thorn in Khrushchev's side. Its prosperity caused discontent among residents of the communist eastern districts. Also, the openness in West Berlin allowed many people from East Germany—and elsewhere in the Eastern Bloc—to escape to freedom.

## The Berlin Wall

On the evening of August 12–13, 1961, East German troops erected a barbed wire fence. It divided western Berlin from eastern Berlin. In the days that followed, cement walls went up as well. These walls stopped free passage from east to west.

## Tanks at the Wall

On October 22, a dispute erupted between the United States and the Soviet Union. The issue was the free passage of U.S. government employees between East and West Berlin.

The United States maintained that agreements reached at Potsdam (at the end of World War II) allowed members of the Allies to travel freely throughout Berlin. To test whether the Soviets would honor this agreement, the U.S. began sending cars carrying U.S. officials across the dividing line. They wanted to see if the Soviets would stop them. If they were stopped, U.S. troops—sometimes riding in tanks—accompanied them across.

On October 27, the USSR responded. It sent some of its own tanks to the entrance of East Berlin. U.S. and Soviet tanks aimed their guns at one another. A fight was narrowly averted. Kennedy and Khrushchev agreed to remove their tanks at the same time.

## Czechoslovakia, 1968

Tensions flared in Europe again in 1968. Czechoslovakia, like Poland and Hungary before it, sought to loosen its ties to the Soviet Union.

Early in the year, the country's conservative leader Antonín Novotný was replaced by Alexander Dubček. Dubček instituted economic reforms. He ended government censorship. As Czechs called for even greater reforms, the Soviet Union became alarmed—just as it had in Poland and Hungary in 1956.

The Soviets feared that changes in Czechoslovakia would spark calls for reform elsewhere in the Eastern Bloc or in the Soviet republics themselves. They were also confident the United States would not intervene, just as it had failed to do before. The new Soviet leader, Leonid Brezhnev, ordered an invasion of Czechoslovakia on August 20, 1968.

By early 1969, resistance had largely disappeared. The Soviet Union replaced Dubček with the conservative Gustáv Husák. Husák reversed Dubček's reforms. Censorship was restored. Government control increased again.

For the Soviets, this was a successful application of the Brezhnev Doctrine. This doctrine pledged to assist communist governments that were in danger of being overthrown.

# China, the Soviet Union, and the Vietnam War

## A Broken Alliance

China and the Soviet Union were once close allies. The Soviet Union supported the Chinese Communist Party from its very start. In 1950, the two countries signed a treaty of friendship and mutual assistance. The Soviets gave China money. They also provided technical help to build China's industry.

Then things changed. Mao greatly admired Stalin. So he was angry when Khrushchev denounced Stalin in 1956. Mao also felt he had "seniority." He had led China since 1949. Khrushchev had only been in power since 1953. In Mao's view, *he* should lead world communism. Not Khrushchev.

## The Split Widens

The gap between the two nations grew wider. Khrushchev feared that Mao wanted to attack Taiwan. He worried this could start a war with the United States. So he refused to give China nuclear weapons.

This refusal captured Mao's main complaint about the Soviets after Stalin died. In Mao's eyes, the Soviets had grown too comfortable. They no longer wanted to risk a clash with the U.S. or other "imperialist" powers. That would threaten their own position.

China also felt the USSR did too little for decolonization in Africa and Asia. It supported wars of independence only weakly. Worse, China argued, the Soviets had built *their own* empire in Europe. They were not truly anti-imperialist.

Other events deepened the rift:

- In 1962, India and China clashed over a border dispute. The USSR backed India.
- In 1969, Soviet and Chinese troops fought each other along their shared border.
- In the late 1960s, China cut off funding for North Vietnam's war against the South. North Vietnam then turned to the Soviet Union for help.

## The U.S. Steps In

The United States saw a chance to benefit from the split. In 1972, President Nixon visited China. He was the first sitting U.S. president to do so. He met with Mao.

This move threatened to isolate the Soviet Union. So the Soviets agreed to a summit in Moscow. Brezhnev and Nixon would meet there in May 1972.

The U.S. then used that Soviet desire for closer ties as leverage. In March 1972, North Vietnam launched an offensive against the South. Nixon threatened to cancel the Moscow Summit. He told the Soviets: force North Vietnam back to the peace table, or no meeting.

## The War Ends

In the end, U.S. efforts to pull out of the war succeeded. At the Paris peace talks, North Vietnam and the United States agreed on a deal. The U.S. would withdraw from South Vietnam in 1973.

The fighting did not stop right away. It continued until 1975. That year, North Vietnam defeated South Vietnam. The country was reunified under a communist government.

In total, the war killed more than one million people.

# Slavery in Africa Before the Transatlantic Trade

## Slavery Already Existed in Africa

European ship captains bought captives from other Africans. Europeans did not bring slavery to Africa. It had existed there for centuries before the triangular trade began.

However, African slavery was different in important ways. The slavery that awaited Africans across the Atlantic was very different from what they knew at home.

## How People Became Enslaved in Africa

Slavery existed in many African societies. There were many ways a person could become enslaved:

- **Punishment for crime.** In some societies, slavery was a penalty for breaking the law.
- **Debt.** In other societies, people could be enslaved to pay a debt. They could also sell their own children into slavery to settle what they owed.
- **Famine and hardship.** In times of famine, parents sometimes sold children to wealthier families. This earned money so the family could survive. It also meant the child would be fed.
- **War.** In many societies, enslaved people were taken as prisoners of war.

## The Purpose of Slavery in African Societies

Africans enslaved people mainly to grow their households. The household was the basic economic unit of society. A family suffered if it did not have enough able-bodied workers for the fields or herds. Slavery provided a solution.

Some enslaved Africans stayed with their slaveholder for life. Others expected to regain their freedom. For example, those enslaved to pay a debt gained freedom once the debt was settled.

Even people enslaved for life could take part fully in household and community life:

- They could marry. Their spouse might be free. Their children would be free.
- They might own property. This included owning enslaved people of their own.
- They were often well respected, especially if they had important knowledge or skills.

Africans saw slavery as an unfortunate fate that could happen to anyone. Being enslaved did not mean a person was inherently different or inferior. The life of an enslaved person was not comfortable or easy. But it was not the same as what we picture when we think of Atlantic plantation slavery.

## Chattel Slavery in the Americas

Slavery in the Americas was different. It was **chattel slavery**. In chattel slavery, one person is owned by another like a piece of property. The enslaved person is treated like an inanimate object.

The enslaved had no status or legal rights as persons. They could be bought, sold, inherited, or given away. They had no right to control their own bodies or their own labor. A slaveholder could compel them to do anything he wished. Their status passed to their children. In all European colonies in the Americas, the child of an enslaved woman was born enslaved.

Chattel slavery also existed in Africa. But it was the **only** form of slavery that existed in the Americas.

## The Trans-Saharan Trade and the Arrival of Europeans

For centuries, Africans participated in the trans-Saharan slave trade. They sold prisoners in North Africa and on the Swahili Coast. These captives were transported to destinations in the Mediterranean or the Middle East.

The arrival of Europeans changed this. Europeans were willing to pay large sums. This shifted the focus of the African slave trade. Africans now captured and enslaved large numbers of other Africans. The goal was to sell them to Europeans for transport across the Atlantic.

Wars were launched against rival peoples solely to take captives. Slave traders led expeditions deep into the interior of the continent. They kidnapped people who lived far away. Africans were not safe in their own homes.

In the eighteenth century, slave traders kidnapped a young Olaudah Equiano and his sister. Later an abolitionist, Equiano was playing at home when strangers climbed over a wall into the courtyard while their parents were gone. The strangers carried the children away. Some people were tricked and sold to European slave traders by their own relatives.

## The March to the Coast

Once captured, people were marched for days to coastal trading posts. At these places, Europeans exchanged goods for human beings. Many died on the way.

Slave traders commonly chained captives together during the journey. They sometimes fixed devices around captives' necks. If a captive escaped, the device would prevent them from lowering their head into streams to drink. They would die of thirst.

Once they reached the coast, the traders stripped them naked and shaved their heads. This kept them free of lice. The traders then greased their bodies with palm oil. This made them look fit and healthy when buyers arrived.

## Slave Trading Ports on the West African Coast

Several slave trading ports flourished on the western coast of Africa from the fifteenth through the eighteenth centuries:

- **Ouidah (Whydah), Grand-Popo, Jaquim, and Porto-Novo** – in modern Benin
- **Badagry** – in Nigeria
- **Little Popo** – in Togo

In these ports, English, Dutch, French, Portuguese, Spanish, Danish, and Swedish traders and sea captains bargained with African slave traders for captives.

Some African city-states and kingdoms grew wealthy from the slave trade. Their rulers protested only if their own people were taken.

King Afonso of Kongo wrote to the king of Portugal. He said that, out of a desire for European goods, his own people were capturing fellow Kongolese and selling them to Portuguese traders. He did not denounce the slave trade. He asked only that the Portuguese bring captives to officials of Kongo first. This would ensure they were not free Kongolese wrongfully seized.

King Gezo of Benin said: "The slave trade is the ruling principle of my people. It is the source and the glory of their wealth . . . the mother lulls the child to sleep with notes of triumph over an enemy reduced to slavery."

## Harm to Those Who Remained in Africa

The transatlantic slave trade harmed those who stayed in Africa as well as those who were taken. Families endured deep emotional trauma from losing loved ones. Fear of falling prey to slave traders pervaded villages throughout West and Central Africa.

Olaudah Equiano recalled that when adults left for the fields, children stationed someone in a tree to watch for kidnappers while the others played.

## Economic Damage to Africa

The African economy suffered as well. The people most likely to be captured were men and women in the prime of life. They had been contributing the greatest share of labor to their communities.

When slave traders captured young adults, no one remained to care for children and the elderly. Fewer people were left to reproduce. According to one model, between 1750 and 1850, no population growth occurred south of the Sahara Desert and north of the Limpopo River. This was due to the loss of people to the slave trade.

To compensate for the disappearance of so many young men, many African ethnic groups adopted **polygyny**. This allowed men to take multiple wives. Young men were the laborers most preferred by plantation owners. The loss of men also meant women had to adopt traditionally male economic roles.

## The Devastating Effects of European Trade Goods

The desire for goods Europeans traded for enslaved people also devastated Africa.

**Textiles.** According to some historians, importing European textiles spurred industrialization in the European textile industry. At the same time, it harmed African cloth producers. They could not compete on quantity or price. Weavers continued to produce goods for local markets. But no continent-wide market for African textiles ever had a chance to develop. Europeans already dominated that field.

**Metals.** Similar consequences hit the African metal industry.

## Long-Lasting Effects

These effects have lasted for centuries. One scholar has shown that the areas from which the most enslaved people were taken are today the poorest in Africa. At the time of the slave trade, those same areas were among the most developed. They are also more prone to civil conflict today than other areas of the continent.

Other studies show that people from ethnic groups most affected by the slave trade are less likely to trust others. People from less affected groups tend to trust more. This may be due at least in part to the slave trade breaking down social and political structures that were meant to protect people.

# 1. Slavery already existed in Africa

European ship captains bought captives from other Africans.

Europeans did not bring slavery to Africa.

It had existed there for centuries before the triangular trade began.

However, African slavery was different in important ways.

The slavery that awaited Africans across the Atlantic was very different from what they knew at home.

 

# 2. How people became enslaved in Africa

Slavery existed in many African societies.

There were many ways a person could become enslaved:

- **Punishment for crime.** Some societies used slavery as a penalty for breaking the law.

- **Debt.** Other societies enslaved people to pay a debt. They could also sell their own children into slavery to settle what they owed.

- **Famine and hardship.** In times of famine, parents sometimes sold children to wealthier families. This earned money so the family could survive. It also meant the child would be fed.

- **War.** Many societies took enslaved people as prisoners of war.

 

# 3. The purpose of slavery in African societies

Africans enslaved people mainly to grow their households.

The household was the basic economic unit of society.

A family suffered if it did not have enough able-bodied workers for the fields or herds.

Slavery provided a solution.

Some enslaved Africans stayed with their slaveholder for life.

Others expected to regain their freedom.

For example, those who owed a debt gained freedom once they settled it.

Even people enslaved for life could take part fully in household and community life:

- They could marry. Their spouse might be free. Their children would be free.

- They might own property. This included owning enslaved people of their own.

- They were often well respected, especially if they had important knowledge or skills.

Africans saw slavery as an unfortunate fate that could happen to anyone.

Being enslaved did not mean a person was inherently different or inferior.

The life of an enslaved person was not comfortable or easy.

But it was not the same as what we picture when we think of Atlantic plantation slavery.

 

# 4. Chattel slavery in the Americas

Slavery in the Americas was different.

It was **chattel slavery**.

In chattel slavery, one person owns another like a piece of property.

The enslaved person is treated like an inanimate object.

The enslaved had no status or legal rights as persons.

They could be bought, sold, inherited, or given away.

They had no right to control their own bodies or their own labor.

A slaveholder could compel them to do anything he wished.

Their status passed to their children.

In all European colonies in the Americas, the child of an enslaved woman was born enslaved.

Chattel slavery also existed in Africa.

But it was the **only** form of slavery that existed in the Americas.

 

# 5. The Trans-Saharan trade and the arrival of Europeans

For centuries, Africans took part in the Trans-Saharan slave trade.

They sold prisoners in North Africa and on the Swahili coast.

Traders transported these captives to destinations in the Mediterranean or the Middle East.

The arrival of Europeans changed this.

Europeans were willing to pay large sums.

This shifted the focus of the African slave trade.

Africans now captured and enslaved large numbers of other Africans.

The goal was to sell them to Europeans for transport across the Atlantic.

Wars broke out against rival peoples solely to take captives.

Slave traders led expeditions deep into the interior of the continent.

They kidnapped people who lived far away.

Africans were not safe in their own homes.

In the eighteenth century, slave traders kidnapped a young Olaudah Equiano and his sister.

Later an abolitionist, Equiano was playing at home when strangers climbed over a wall into the courtyard while their parents were gone.

The strangers carried the children away.

Some people were tricked and sold to European slave traders by their own relatives.

 

# 6. The march to the coast

Once captured, people marched for days to coastal trading posts.

At these places, Europeans exchanged goods for human beings.

Many died on the way.

Slave traders commonly chained captives together during the journey.

They sometimes fixed devices around captives' necks.

If a captive escaped, the device would stop them from lowering their head into streams to drink.

They would die of thirst.

Once they reached the coast, the traders stripped them naked and shaved their heads.

This kept them free of lice.

The traders then greased their bodies with palm oil.

This made them look fit and healthy when buyers arrived.

 

# 7. Slave trading ports on the West African coast

Several slave trading ports flourished on the western coast of Africa from the fifteenth through the eighteenth centuries:

- **Ouidah (Whydah), Grand-Popo, Jaquim, and Porto-Novo** – in modern Benin

- **Badagry** – in Nigeria

- **Little Popo** – in Togo

In these ports, English, Dutch, French, Portuguese, Spanish, Danish, and Swedish traders and sea captains bargained with African slave traders for captives.

Some African city-states and kingdoms grew wealthy from the slave trade.

Their rulers protested only if their own people were taken.

King Afonso of Kongo wrote to the King of Portugal.

He said that, out of a desire for European goods, his own people were capturing fellow Kongolese and selling them to Portuguese traders.

He did not denounce the slave trade.

He asked only that the Portuguese bring captives to officials of Kongo first.

This would ensure they were not free Kongolese wrongfully seized.

King Gezo of Benin said: "The slave trade is the ruling principle of my people. It is the source and the glory of their wealth . . . the mother lulls the child to sleep with notes of triumph over an enemy reduced to slavery."

 

# 8. Harm to those who remained in Africa

The transatlantic slave trade harmed those who stayed in Africa as well as those who were taken.

Families endured deep emotional trauma from losing loved ones.

Fear of falling prey to slave traders pervaded villages throughout West and Central Africa.

Olaudah Equiano recalled that when adults left for the fields, children stationed someone in a tree to watch for kidnappers while the others played.

 

# 9. Economic damage to Africa

The African economy suffered as well.

The people most likely to be captured were men and women in the prime of life.

They had been contributing the greatest share of labor to their communities.

When slave traders captured young adults, no one remained to care for children and the elderly.

Fewer people were left to reproduce.

According to one model, between 1750 and 1850, the population did not grow south of the Sahara Desert and north of the Limpopo River.

This was due to the loss of people to the slave trade.

To compensate for the disappearance of so many young men, many African ethnic groups adopted **polygyny**.

This allowed men to take multiple wives.

Young men were the laborers most preferred by plantation owners.

The loss of men also meant women had to adopt traditionally male economic roles.

 

# 10. The devastating effects of European trade goods

The desire for goods Europeans traded for enslaved people also devastated Africa.

**Textiles.** According to some historians, importing European textiles spurred industrialization in the European textile industry. At the same time, it harmed African cloth producers. They could not compete on quantity or price. Weavers continued to produce goods for local markets. But no continent-wide market for African textiles ever had a chance to develop. Europeans already dominated that field.

**Metals.** Similar consequences hit the African metal industry.

 

# 11. Long-lasting effects

These effects have lasted for centuries.

One scholar has shown that the areas from which the most enslaved people were taken are today the poorest in Africa.

At the time of the slave trade, those same areas were among the most developed.

They are also more prone to civil conflict today than other areas of the continent.

Other studies show that people from ethnic groups most affected by the slave trade are less likely to trust others.

People from less affected groups tend to trust more.

This may be due at least in part to the slave trade breaking down social and political structures that were meant to protect people.

# Liberalism

## What Is Liberalism?

**Liberalism** is a political philosophy. It grew from Enlightenment ideas. It was born in the revolutionary struggles of the 1800s and late 1700s. Like nationalism, it traces its roots to the Enlightenment.

Its core goal is **freedom from restraint**. This means:

- Freedom of expression
- Popular sovereignty (the people hold power)
- Representative government
- Protection of private property
- Protection of civil rights

## Liberalism Changed Over Time

The meaning of "liberal" has shifted over the centuries.

In the 19th century, liberals **opposed** government intervention in daily life.

Today, in the United States, people called liberals generally support:

- Government assistance for the poor
- Government action to promote equality

So a 21st-century liberal and a 19th-century liberal would often disagree on the role of government.

## Liberalism and Nationalism

These two ideas are **not** mutually exclusive. A person can hold both at once. For example, the nationalist leader **Mazzini** also adopted many liberal principles.

Over time, thinkers split liberalism into two branches:

- **Political liberalism** (rooted in John Locke)
- **Economic liberalism** (rooted in Adam Smith)

---

## Political Liberalism

Political liberalism grew from the ideas of **John Locke**. Locke stressed two key concepts:

1. The **consent of the governed** – rulers need the people's agreement to rule.
2. **Natural rights** – every person has a right to life, liberty, and property.

From these ideas, political liberalism promotes:

- A **limited government** that cannot overreach its power.
- The right to **oppose any authority** that lacks the people's consent.
- A **written constitution** that sets limits on government and guarantees rights for all citizens.

In the 18th century, two more principles became central:

- **Religious toleration** – no single faith is forced on everyone.
- **Separation of church and state** – religion and government stay apart.

These ideas shaped major revolutionary movements in:

- Britain's North American colonies (the United States)
- Haiti
- France

Each of these revolutions produced a **written constitution**. Each one declared that the people hold sovereignty.

The Enlightenment idea of natural rights was tested again and again through revolution. Over time, it became a lasting commitment to two principles:

- Consent of the governed
- Equality before the law

These principles defined liberal political thought in the 19th century.

---

## John Stuart Mill and Individual Freedom

One of the most famous liberals of the 1800s was **John Stuart Mill**, an English philosopher. He argued that individual rights must be protected from censorship and tyranny.

In 1859, he published his classic work, ***On Liberty***. In it, he made two key points:

- **Toleration** is essential.
- Multiple ethical codes can coexist peacefully in one society.

Mill believed people should make their own ethical choices. Government should not intrude or obstruct those personal decisions.

Mill also championed **equality**. He was a strong supporter of women's rights. His essay, ***On the Subjection of Women***, played an important role in the 19th-century women's rights movement.

---

## Economic Liberalism and Adam Smith

Economic liberalism came from a different source: the Scottish economist **Adam Smith**. His theories helped shape the growing capitalism of his era.

Smith argued for **laissez-faire**. This is the idea that economic affairs should be free of government interference.

In 1759, he wrote ***The Theory of Moral Sentiments***. In it, he made a key claim:

- When people pursue their own self-interest in a free market, unseen forces guide the outcome.
- He called these forces an **"invisible hand."**
- Any government interference would only **disrupt** this natural process.

Smith's logic was simple. If individuals are free to seek financial success without government restraint, everyone benefits from the greater prosperity that follows.

Although Smith focused mainly on economics, he shared a core belief with Mill and Locke:

- Freedom from government restraint is essential.
- Protection of natural rights underpins any successful government.

Belgium was one of the smallest industrialized nations in Europe. Its lawmakers did not think it had enough money or power. They believed Belgium could not afford a colony.

# Art and Literature in the Industrial City

The industrial city was more than a place to live, work, and have fun. It also shaped art and literature. In the late 1800s, artists and writers made the city their subject. Industrialization changed how people made goods and moved things. It also changed what they created in culture.

---

## Romanticism: Nature Against the Machine

The first big cultural response to industrialization was **romanticism**. This movement started in the late 1700s and early 1800s. Romantics valued emotion and imagination. They wrote about nature, ordinary people, exotic places, ancient times, and the supernatural.

Romantic artists stressed the beauty of nature. They also showed its awe-inspiring power. They criticized cities and industrial growth. They said these things harmed people and the land.

William Blake called England's factories "dark satanic mills." This phrase captured the romantic view of modern life perfectly.

---

## Realism: Life as It Really Was

Another key movement was **realism**. Realists showed everyday life in the present day. They did not focus on exotic or ancient themes like romantics did. They depicted life exactly as it was. Sometimes that meant showing its uglier side.

### Realist Painters

Some realist painters chose rural scenes:

- **Rosa Bonheur** painted horse fairs in the countryside.
- **Jean-François Millet** painted oxen straining at the plow and men sowing fields.

Other realists focused on modern cities and their people:

- **John Sloan** and **George Luks** painted barrooms from the inside.
- They also painted crowded streets in working-class neighborhoods.

### Realist Writers

Writers also made the city their subject. One of the greatest realist writers was Britain's **Charles Dickens**. His novels were widely read. He showed the hard lives of poor, working-class, and middle-class city dwellers with sympathy. His scenes took place in foundling homes, prisons, impoverished neighborhoods, and dark streets.

Some critics said Dickens was unrealistic about how virtuous he made the poor seem. But his books (and his activism) raised awareness. They especially highlighted the plight of children. They helped bring about some social change.

Other writers focused even more on life's shabbier side:

- **Fyodor Dostoyevsky** (Russia) described the streets of St. Petersburg. He wrote about rundown quarters where the poor were forced to live. He also wrote about cheap saloons where they sought relief.
- **Honoré de Balzac** (France) depicted the seedy side of life in French cities. He often focused on stories of crime.
- **Gustave Flaubert** (France) wrote *Madame Bovary*. It tells of a rural doctor's young wife. Her desire for consumer goods and urban pleasures leads to her ruin.
- **Kate Chopin** (America) addressed women who felt stifled by married life and the social rules of the time.

---

## Naturalism: Trapped by Environment and Heredity

In the late 1800s, a new style emerged. It was called **naturalism**. It joined realism and then surpassed it.

Naturalism had key features:

- Depictions were detached and impersonal.
- Characters' actions were shaped by their environment.
- Characters often could not control what happened to them.

The French novelist **Émile Zola** created naturalism. His many works show people trapped by their surroundings or their heredity. These characters act in ways they cannot be fully blamed for.

### *Thérèse Raquin* (1867)

Zola's first naturalistic novel was *Thérèse Raquin*. He published it in installments in the magazine *L'Artiste* in 1867. Here is what happens:

- Thérèse is an orphan.
- The woman who raised her forces her to marry that woman's sickly son.
- Thérèse does not love him.
- She eventually murders him, with the help of a brutish man she is drawn to by irresistible sexual impulses.

Literary critics were shocked by *Thérèse Raquin*. They also decried it as immoral. They reacted the same way to later works of naturalism.

### *McTeague* (1899)

American readers were similarly shocked by Frank Norris's novel *McTeague*. Here is the story:

- McTeague is a dentist.
- He marries Trina, though his friend was in love with her.
- The friend takes revenge. He destroys McTeague's dental practice.
- McTeague steals money from Trina and runs away.
- When he returns, he has spent all the stolen money.
- Trina refuses to help him.
- He beats her to death.
- He then flees from the law, with his former friend in pursuit.

The novel ends in the desert. McTeague is stranded there. He is handcuffed to the body of his friend, whom he has killed.

In the world of *McTeague*, people are greedy, faithless, and violent. There is no escape from life's horrors.

# Contract Labor and Debt Bondage

## A New Way to Control Workers

Slavery and serfdom disappeared from the industrialized world in the nineteenth century. But people still needed a long-term labor force. They wanted workers for farms and factories. Two new systems filled that need: **contract labor** and **debt bondage**.

---

## What Is Contract Labor?

Contract labor means people sign a contract. The contract says they will work in exchange for a fee. This system still exists today.

One form of contract labor is called **indentured servitude**. A person pledges to work for an agreed period of time. In return, they receive an agreed form of compensation.

Indentured servants are not enslaved. But while their contract is active, their employers have nearly total control over them. The servant cannot leave the job.

---

## What Is Debt Bondage?

**Debt bondage** works differently. A person owes money to a creditor. To pay off that debt, the person must work for the creditor. Or they may provide someone else to do the work. They keep working until the debt is fully repaid through labor.

Indentured servitude and debt bondage are similar. Both were common in the later nineteenth century. But both differ from slavery in one key way: theoretically, the bondage will end at a set point in time.

---

## Indentured Servitude in the United States

In colonial America, indentured servitude was very common. Many Europeans used it to pay for passage to North America. By the middle of the nineteenth century, the practice had largely died out in the U.S. But it still existed in a few places.

**Hawaii.** Plantation owners hired contract laborers from Portugal, China, Korea, Japan, and the Philippines. These workers grew crops, especially sugarcane.

**Chinese immigrants in the U.S.** Many Chinese people came to the United States as contract laborers. But they were not working under a contract with their employer. Instead, they had agreed to work for one of their compatriots. The purpose was to pay for their passage to the United States.

Many of these workers were brought abroad by the **Six Companies**. This was a Chinese-owned business formed to transport Chinese immigrants to North America. Workers had to repay their debt to the company before they were allowed to return home.

---

## Contract Labor Around the World

Other parts of the world also relied on contract labor after slavery was abolished.

**Australia.** During the nineteenth century, Australia depended on indentured laborers from Pacific islands. These included the Solomon Islands, Tuvalu, Samoa, and the Gilbert Islands (now called Kiribati).

**A global trade in laborers.** A large trade provided Chinese and Indian laborers to many regions. They were sent to work in:

- Latin America
- The Caribbean
- Southeast Asia
- European colonies in Africa

These laborers faced terrible conditions. They were underpaid. They were overworked. They were brutally disciplined. They received only enough food to keep them working.

Reports of this poor treatment reached many industrialized countries. Those countries then ended their participation in the trade.

**Britain** prohibited its ships from carrying Asian laborers to Cuba and Peru. These were two of the main destinations for such workers.

In **1874**, Portugal followed Britain's example. It blocked the trade from being carried on in Macao. Macao was a Portuguese colony in Asia. Many Chinese laborers had been shipped from there to other parts of the world.

---

## Debt Bondage in the Late Nineteenth Century

Debt bondage was also a common source of labor in some regions during this period.

**Japan, 1880s.** Japan faced an economic depression. Many families went bankrupt. Some starved. In response, parents "rented" their children to factories. This especially affected daughters. The girls were given food and shelter. Any money they earned was sent home to their parents.

Daughters might also be hired out to brothels. Some dutiful daughters made this decision themselves. They did it to spare their parents the pain of choosing for them.

**The United States.** Debt bondage was a common tool used by southern farmers. It kept a labor force at their disposal. This included African American people and poor White people. Debt bondage also trapped many Asian laborers who had immigrated to South America. Some were stuck even after their contracts had expired.

---

## When Escape Was Nearly Impossible

In some places, debt bondage was almost impossible to break free from.

**Sharecropping and tenant farming.** Sharecroppers and tenant farmers worked on other people's land. They depended entirely on the harvest for their income. Before the harvest came in, they needed food and other necessities. They bought these items on credit from a local store. That store was usually owned by the landlord.

They also often had to buy seed from the landlord. And they used equipment that belonged to the landlord. After the harvest, they sold their crops. Then they repaid their debts.

But here was the trap: prices at the store were very high. The interest charged by the store owner was also very high. So the income from the harvest was not enough to cover the full debt. The unpaid portion was added to what they owed for the next harvest. This cycle repeated year after year.

**Scrip.** Some employers paid their workers with scrip. Scrip is a substitute for money. It could only be exchanged at one place: the store owned by that employer. Workers could not shop anywhere else. So they had no choice but to go into debt again and again.

**Japanese brothels.** The young women there were not paid in scrip. But every cost was recorded against them. This included clothing, food, and everything else provided for them. A woman could not go free until she repaid two things: the original sum that had been exchanged for her, and the total cost of her upkeep while she was there.

# European Migration in the 1800s and Early 1900s

## Who Left Europe?

Between the 1800s and the early 1900s, about **60 million Europeans** left their homes. They wanted better economic chances on other continents.

Most came from poor farming areas. Southern Italy and Sicily were common origins. These regions had little industry.

About **28 million** of these migrants went to the United States. Most arrived between **1890 and 1914**. The majority were peasant farmers from southern and eastern Europe.

Germany and Ireland also sent many immigrants. In fact, those two countries had led immigration in the first half of the 1800s.

Not everyone left for money. Some fled religious persecution. Jewish people in the Russian empire faced discrimination and anti-Semitism. This often turned into violent attacks called **pogroms**. People were killed. Property was destroyed.

Others who emigrated included:

- Political dissidents
- Craftspeople displaced by industrialization

## Where Did They Go?

After the United States, these countries received the most European immigrants:

- Argentina
- Brazil
- Chile
- Uruguay

About **4.5 million** emigrants went to Argentina. At one point, they made up **30 percent** of its population. Latin America attracted many Italians and Germans. It also drew Spanish and Portuguese settlers.

Canada received about **5.1 million** people between the 1850s and the 1920s.

Other common destinations included:

- Australia
- New Zealand
- South Africa

Gold discoveries made some places especially attractive. Gold was found in **Australia in 1851**. It was found in **South Africa in 1886**.

## What Work Did Immigrants Do?

European immigrants took on many different jobs once they arrived.

Here is a breakdown by group:

- **Many** worked in factories.
- **Jewish people** were especially active in the garment industry, such as in New York City.
- **Polish and other eastern Europeans** worked in steel mills in Pittsburgh and in Chicago's stockyards (in the U.S.).
- **Portuguese** often worked in fishing. In New England, they also worked alongside French Canadians in textile mills.
- **Italians** did a variety of work: agriculture, mining, and building trades.
- **Welsh people** found jobs as miners in the West.
- **Irish immigrants** worked in mines, built railroads, and labored in factories across the United States.
- **Women** from all these groups entered domestic service.

## How Were Immigrants Received?

The response to newcomers often depended on their ethnicity.

In the United States:

- The "foreign" ways of Germans and eastern European Christians might be mocked. But they were largely accepted.
- Irish newcomers faced rejection at first. Most were Roman Catholics. They arrived in large numbers in the 1840s and 1850s. The U.S. was mostly Protestant then. By the second half of the 1800s, though, Irish people and their children had become politicians, business owners, and police officers.
- Jewish people and Italians were more recent arrivals. They often faced discrimination. Anti-Semitism was widespread.

## New Immigration Laws in the U.S.

By the end of the 1800s, many native-born Protestants of northern European ancestry called for changes to immigration laws.

In **1924**, Congress passed the **Johnson-Reed Act**. This law did two main things:

1. It set a **quota** on the total number of immigrants allowed into the U.S. from outside the Western Hemisphere.
2. It limited each nationality's share to **2 percent** of that group already living in the U.S. in 1890.

This meant a person could be turned away if their nationality's quota was full, even if the overall limit had not been reached.

Why did this matter? Before 1890, most immigrants came from northern and western Europe. Fewer came from southern or eastern Europe. So the 2 percent rule allowed far more English, Irish, and German people to enter than Italian, Polish, or Russian Jewish people.

Immigration from **Asia** was banned. The only exception was the U.S. territory of the Philippines.

## A Different Story in Latin America

Latin America told a very different story.

Argentina and Uruguay had never had large populations. Why? They lacked their neighbors' mineral wealth. Their climates were not suited to growing sugar or coffee. So European immigrants were a welcome boost there.

Brazil and Venezuela took a deliberate approach. They sought out European immigrants on purpose. Their goal was to make their predominantly African, Native American, and biracial population more White.

# Unions and Politics in the 19th Century

## How Unions Grew Differently Around the World

In Britain and the United States, unions grew on their own. They did not depend on politics.

In Germany, France, and Russia, things were different. Political ideas pushed unions to grow. The main idea behind this growth was **socialism**.

Today, socialism means the government owns the tools and factories that make goods. In the 1800s, it meant many different things. But all forms shared three beliefs:

- They disliked free-market capitalism with no rules.
- They wanted to help poor people live better lives.
- They believed the government should fix problems caused by industry.

## Utopian Socialism (Early 1800s)

In the early 1800s, **utopian socialism** was the leading form. It focused on building a perfect society.

French thinkers like Henri de Saint-Simon and Charles Fourier wrote about ideal societies. These societies were based on sharing and working together. They wanted to change all of society. They pushed for new ideas such as:

- Communal housing
- Free love
- Women's rights

All of these ideas were radical at the time.

Some reformers tried to build real communities based on these ideals. Robert Owen was a British textile manufacturer. He put some of these ideas into practice in two places:

- **New Lanark**, a village in Britain, where workers lived near his father-in-law's mill
- **New Harmony**, a town in Indiana, USA

In these communities, residents worked eight-hour days. They lived in decent housing. They raised their children together as a group.

## Scientific Socialism (Mid-1800s)

By the middle of the 1800s, utopian socialism had mostly faded. It was replaced by **scientific socialism**.

The term "scientific socialism" was first used by Pierre-Joseph Proudhon. He was a French economist and philosopher. He used it to mean ordering society based on reason. Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels made the term famous.

In 1848, Marx and Engels published *The Communist Manifesto*. That same year, political revolutions swept across Europe. These revolutions changed voting rights for men in France and Prussia.

By the end of the 1800s, men in France and Germany had used their votes to change their countries. (Germany united with Prussia in 1871 to form the most powerful German-speaking state.) Many people supported the socialist ideas written by Marx and Engels.

## What Marx and Engels Believed

Marx and Engels believed history changed through conflict between social classes. In the age of industry, this conflict would happen between two groups:

- **The bourgeoisie** – owners of factories, mines, and railroads. They made wealth.
- **The proletariat** – underpaid workers whose labor was exploited by the owners.

Marx and Engels believed capitalism would end when the poor rose up in revolution. They would overthrow their bourgeois oppressors. After that:

- All people would be equal.
- All property would be shared.
- Class divisions and class conflict would disappear forever.

This philosophy became known as **Marxism**. It formed the core belief of most socialists in the second half of the 1800s.

## Putting Ideas into Action

Marx never tried to put his own philosophy into practice. But during the Second Industrial Revolution, many workers used his ideas. They organized unions and built political parties based on them.

In 1864, socialists founded the **International Workingmen's Association (IWA)** in London. Many different types of socialists joined the IWA, including Marx. Conflict soon arose over several issues:

- Some wanted to use violence to force change.
- Others wanted peaceful, democratic methods.

Those who favored peaceful means are often called **social democrats**.

## Social Democratic Parties

One of the largest and most influential social democratic parties was the **German Social Democratic Party**. It formed in 1875. Its goals included:

- Passing laws to improve working conditions
- Reducing the number of hours people worked
- Building trade unions
- Protecting workers through new laws

Many of its members were elected to the German parliament.

Similar parties formed elsewhere:

- The **Federation of the Socialist Workers of France (FSWF)** was established in 1879.
- The **Social Democratic Party of Austria** was founded in 1889.

## Revolutionary Parties

These social democratic parties competed for workers' support against more radical groups.

The **French Workers' Party** was established in 1880. It offered an alternative to the slower, gradual path favored by the FSWF.

In Russia:

- The **Russian Social Democratic Labor Party** formed in 1898. It united many smaller socialist organizations. Most Russian groups that followed orthodox Marxism joined it.
- The **Socialist Revolutionary Party** formed in 1902. It assassinated government officials. It ignored Marx's focus on factory workers and tried to organize peasants too.

The **Bolshevik faction** of the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party advocated revolution. In 1917, it gained control of the Russian government.

## The Role of Government: A Key Debate

Another major conflict among socialists was about government's role in building a socialist state.

Marx wrote that government would eventually disappear once class divisions were gone and equality was achieved. But he also said something else. Until that point, a government run by workers would be needed to manage society.

Some socialists feared this new government would just create a new group of rulers who oppressed people. They believed government should be abolished entirely. This ideology is called **anarchism**.

One of the leading anarchists of the 1800s was **Mikhail Bakunin**, a Russian revolutionary. He joined the IWA in 1868. But he clashed with Marx over the role of government. In 1872, at the Fifth Congress of the IWA, his disagreement with Marx led to his expulsion from the group.

## Why Business Owners Opposed Socialism

Business owners and members of the middle and upper classes disapproved of socialist and anarchist movements. They feared them.

They believed business owners did a valuable job:

- They provided goods and services at reasonable prices.
- They made the economy grow.
- They kept their countries strong and competitive.

Because they took on financial risk, they believed they were entitled to earn a fair profit. To keep prices low while earning that profit, they could not pay wages as high as workers wanted.

## Other Arguments Against Socialism

Opponents of socialism and anarchism made more points:

- Workers were free to accept job terms or leave if unhappy.
- If owners could not earn a profit, they would not take the financial risks the economy needed.
- If people could not own private property, they would lose the motivation to work.
- Violence and destroying property helped no one.

They argued workers would be better off in another way. They should improve their lives through education. They should build habits of thrift and self-discipline. This would help them and their children. It was better than listening to demagogues who preached disloyalty to employers. Those demagogues spun utopian fantasies about workers' paradises that could never be real.

# Unions and Politics in the 19th Century


## Table of Contents

1. How unions grew differently around the world
2. Utopian socialism (early 1800s)
3. Scientific socialism (mid-1800s)
4. What Marx and Engels believed
5. Putting ideas into action
6. Social democratic parties
7. Revolutionary parties
8. The role of government: a key debate
9. Why business owners opposed socialism
10. Other arguments against socialism


---

## How Unions Grew Differently Around the World

In **Britain** and the **United States**, unions grew on their own.

They did not need politics to survive or grow.


In **Germany**, **France**, and **Russia**, things worked differently.

Political ideas pushed unions forward.

The main idea behind this growth was **socialism**.


Today, socialism means the government owns factories and tools.

It means the state makes goods for people.


In the 1800s, it meant many different things.

But all forms shared three beliefs:

- They did not like free-market capitalism with no rules.
- They wanted to help poor people live better lives.
- They believed the government should fix problems caused by industry.


---

## Utopian Socialism (Early 1800s)

In the early 1800s, **utopian socialism** led the way.

It focused on building a perfect society from scratch.


French thinkers wrote about ideal societies.

Two of them were:

- **Henri de Saint-Simon**
- **Charles Fourier**

They based their ideas on sharing and working together.

They wanted to change all of society at once.

They pushed for new ideas such as:

- Communal housing where families shared a home.
- Free love, which meant no rules about marriage.
- Women's rights, including equal pay and education.


All of these ideas were radical at the time.

Most people found them shocking or dangerous.


Some reformers tried to build real communities.

They wanted to test these ideals in daily life.


**Robert Owen** was a British textile maker.

He put some of these ideas into practice in two places:

- **New Lanark**, a village in Britain. Workers lived near his father-in-law's mill there.
- **New Harmony**, a town in Indiana, United States.


In these communities:

- Residents worked eight-hour days.
- They lived in decent housing with clean water.
- They raised their children together as a group.
- No single family owned the home or the land.


---

## Scientific Socialism (Mid-1800s)

By the middle of the 1800s, utopian socialism had mostly faded.

People found its perfect-society plans too hard to reach.

A new form took its place: **scientific socialism**.


The term "scientific socialism" first showed up in writing by **Pierre-Joseph Proudhon**.

He was a French economist and thinker.

He used the word to mean ordering society based on reason and evidence.

**Karl Marx** and **Friedrich Engels** later made the term well known.


In **1848**, Marx and Engels published *"The Communist Manifesto."*

That same year, political uprisings swept across Europe.

These uprisings changed voting rights for men in France and Prussia.

For the first time, ordinary men could vote on national issues.


By the end of the 1800s, men in France and Germany used their votes to change their countries.

Germany united with Prussia in **1871**.

It became the most powerful German-speaking state in Europe.

Many people supported the socialist ideas written by Marx and Engels.

They saw those ideas as a path to real power for workers.


---

## What Marx and Engels Believed

Marx and Engels believed history changed through conflict.

This conflict happened between social classes.

In the age of industry, two groups clashed:

- **The bourgeoisie** – owners of factories, mines, and railroads. They made wealth from other people's work.
- **The proletariat** – underpaid workers whose labor fed the owners' profits.


Marx and Engels believed capitalism would end through revolution.

The poor would rise up and overthrow their bourgeois rulers.

After that, they said:

- All people would be equal in status and pay.
- All property would be shared by the community.
- Class divisions and class conflict would disappear for good.


This way of thinking became known as **Marxism**.

It formed the core belief of most socialists in the second half of the 1800s.

Workers across Europe read Marx's books and spread his ideas.


---

## Putting Ideas into Action

Marx never tried to put his own philosophy into practice.

He stayed a writer and thinker for his whole life.


But during the **second industrial revolution**, many workers used his ideas.

They organized unions around them.

They built political parties based on them.


In **1864**, socialists founded the **International Workingmen's Association** in London.

Many different types of socialists joined this group.

Marx himself was a member and held a key role.

Conflict soon arose over several issues:

- Some wanted to use violence to force change.
- Others wanted peaceful, democratic methods like voting and strikes.


Those who favored peaceful means are often called **social democrats**.

They believed workers could win rights through the ballot box.


---

## Social Democratic Parties

One of the largest social democratic parties was the **German Social Democratic Party**.

It formed in **1875**.

Its goals included:

- Passing laws to improve working conditions in factories.
- Cutting down the number of hours people worked each week.
- Building strong trade unions across all trades.
- Protecting workers through new safety and pay laws.


Many of its members won seats in the German parliament.

They used those seats to push for worker-friendly laws.


Similar parties formed in other countries:

- The **Federation of the Socialist Workers of France** was set up in **1879**. It pushed for shorter hours and better pay in French factories.
- The **Social Democratic Party of Austria** was founded in **1889**. It focused on organizing industrial workers in Vienna and other cities.


---

## Revolutionary Parties

These social democratic parties competed for workers' support.

More radical groups challenged them from the left.

They promised faster, more dramatic change.


The **French Workers' Party** was set up in **1880**.

It offered a different path to the slower one favored by the French Federation.

Its members wanted direct action, not just voting.


In Russia, two major groups formed:

- The **Russian Social Democratic Labor Party** formed in **1898**. It united many smaller socialist groups under one roof. Most Russian groups that followed orthodox Marxism joined it.
- The **Socialist Revolutionary Party** formed in **1902**. It killed government officials to force change. It ignored Marx's focus on factory workers and tried to organize farm workers too.


The **Bolshevik faction** of the Russian Social Democratic Labor Party pushed for armed revolution.

It rejected slow, gradual reform as a path forward.

In **1917**, it gained control of the Russian government.

It went on to build the first socialist state in history.


---

## The Role of Government: A Key Debate

Another big fight among socialists was about the role of government.

They disagreed on how much power a new state should hold.


Marx wrote that government would eventually go away.

This would happen once class divisions were gone and equality was reached.

But he also said something else.

Until that point, a government run by workers would be needed to manage society.

It would protect the revolution from outside attack.


Some socialists feared this new government would create a problem.

They worried it would just build a new group of rulers who oppressed people.

They believed government should be scrapped entirely.

No state. No bosses. No police. Just free communities.

This way of thinking is called **anarchism**.


One of the leading anarchists of the 1800s was **Mikhail Bakunin**, a Russian revolutionary.

He joined the International Workingmen's Association in **1868**.

But he clashed with Marx over the role of government.

Marx wanted a workers' state to lead the change.

Bakunin wanted no state at all, not even for a short time.


In **1872**, at the fifth congress of the group, his disagreement led to his removal.

The split between Marxists and anarchists shaped politics for decades after.


---

## Why Business Owners Opposed Socialism

Business owners and members of the middle and upper classes did not approve of socialist movements.

They also feared anarchist groups that used violence.

They saw both as threats to their way of life.


They believed business owners did a valuable job for society:

- They provided goods and services at fair prices.
- They made the economy grow year after year.
- They kept their countries strong and competitive on world markets.


Because they took on financial risk, they felt entitled to earn a fair profit.

If a factory failed, the owner lost everything.

To keep prices low while earning that profit, they could not pay wages as high as workers wanted.

They saw this as a simple matter of survival for their business.


---

- Workers were free to accept job terms or leave if unhappy. No one forced them to stay.

They argued workers would be better off in another way.

This would help them and their children over time.

It was better than listening to loud talkers who preached disloyalty to employers.

Those talkers spun dreamy stories about workers' perfect worlds that could never be real in practice.

# The Zimmermann Telegram

On March 1, 1917, a secret message was made public. It was called the **Zimmermann Telegram**. This event made tensions between Germany and the United States even worse.

Germany's foreign minister, Arthur Zimmermann, had sent this message to Mexico. He offered Mexico a deal.

Here is what happened before that. In 1916, there were many disturbances along the U.S.–Mexico border. A man named Francisco "Pancho" Villa was behind them. He attacked towns in the United States. The U.S. Army sent thousands of troops to the border. Their job was to track down Villa.

Germany saw an opportunity. It wanted Mexico to cause more border trouble if war broke out with the United States. More disturbances would mean more U.S. troops stuck at the border. Those troops could not be sent to fight in Europe.

In return, Germany made a promise. If Germany won the war, it would give Mexico back three regions: **Texas**, **New Mexico**, and **Arizona**. Mexico had lost that territory in 1848 after a war with the United States.

---

# Why Mexico Could Not Join

In reality, Mexico could not take part in this plan. Even if it wanted to, it was too divided. In 1917, violent conflict raged among many revolutionary factions inside Mexico. Villa's forces were just one of them.

To understand why, we need to look back at how the trouble started.

---

# The Mexican Revolution Begins (1910–1913)

In 1910, a liberal politician named **Francisco Madero** ran for president of Mexico. He challenged **Porfirio Díaz**. Díaz had held the presidency continuously since 1884. His regime was dictatorial. It favored wealthy landowners and business owners.

Díaz won the election. The vote was rigged. He then had Madero arrested. This act sparked uprisings across the country.

In 1911, Díaz was forced to resign. He went into exile.

Madero was declared president. But he failed to deliver the reforms people expected. A new revolt broke out against his government. In 1913, Madero was forced to give up his office.

A general named **Victoriano Huerta** replaced him. Huerta commanded rebellious forces within the Mexican army. Soon after taking power, he had Madero executed.

Huerta tried to rule like a dictator. Opposition rose quickly.

---

# The Factions Fight (1913–1914)

In the south, **Emiliano Zapata** led a rebellion. His followers were Indigenous peasants. They wanted a program of land reform.

In the north, three men led the revolution: **Venustiano Carranza**, **Alvaro Obregon**, and **Pancho Villa**.

U.S. president Woodrow Wilson backed Carranza. He supplied Carranza's forces with munitions. Wilson also used this moment to order U.S. marines into Mexico. His stated goal was to prevent damage to U.S.-owned property. In April 1914, the U.S. Navy took control of the Mexican port of **Veracruz**.

Throughout the summer of 1914, the rebel factions fought each other. Each leader wanted to replace Huerta. In July, Huerta fled into exile.

Carranza declared himself president. Villa and Zapata objected.

---

# Villa's Raid and the U.S. Response (1916)

In March 1916, Villa attacked the town of **Columbus, New Mexico**. This was retaliation for U.S. support of Carranza.

Wilson responded by sending five thousand troops across the border. Their mission: capture Villa.

Villa evaded them. Within a year, the U.S. troops had retreated home.

This invasion damaged relations between the United States and Carranza. He refused to accept what he saw as an insult to Mexican sovereignty.

By 1917, Carranza was firmly in power. But rebellion continued. Villa led fighters in the northern state of **Chihuahua**. Zapata led fighters in **Morelos** in the south.

---

# The U.S. Reacts and Enters the War

So when Germany approached Carranza with its offer of an alliance against the United States, he was not in a position to accept it. He did not have the control or the stability to do so.

But when the telegram became public, the United States was furious. The country was not yet at war. And Germany was already planning how to break up its territory.

Money and business also pushed the U.S. toward war. American banks had extended loans to the European Allies. If Germany won, those loans would go unpaid. So the banks supported U.S. involvement. Businesses saw a different benefit. They hoped that if the United States helped the Allies win, the Allies would grant them greater access to global markets.

Popular support for going to war against Germany swelled fast.

In **April 1917**, the United States entered the conflict on the side of the Allied powers. The country was already angry over the sinking of the **Lusitania** and the **Sussex**. The Zimmermann Telegram added fuel to that fire.

# The Home Front in World War I

## Adapting to a Long War

The war was long. It touched every part of life. Every country had to change how it worked at home.

In Britain and France, many young men joined the army. Some volunteered. Others were forced to serve through conscription. This meant skilled workers left their factories. Factories needed new workers. Training those workers took time. Production slowed down.

Germany faced a different problem. The Allied blockade cut off its raw materials. Germany had to find new sources. It could not rely on the old supply routes.

## Shells and Politics

Production problems became political problems. In 1915, British commanders made an accusation. They said they were turned back in an attack because they lacked artillery shells. This was called the "shell crisis."

It raised a hard question. Who was to blame? The government had not ordered enough shells? Or the workers had not worked hard enough?

The British government blamed the army. It said the military had not placed large enough orders. Shell output then rose in 1915. This happened in Britain and in every other combatant nation.

## Pressure on the British Government

The British government faced heavy pressure during the war. The Liberal Party was in power. But this party had always been against war. World War I threw the party into confusion.

The shell crisis hurt the government's image. So did the failures at Gallipoli. Both made the government look weak.

David Lloyd George added to the tension. He served as minister of munitions. He was also a Liberal. He kept maneuvering against the prime minister. These divisions grew until the end of the war.

## The United States and War Production

The United States entered the war later. Its government moved to control industry in a new way. It created the **War Industries Board (WIB)**.

Barnard Baruch, a financier, ran the WIB. The board controlled prices. It organized production to support the war effort.

But the U.S. had never used central planning before. It had no experience with centralized economic control. So it could not command war production the way Britain could.

The WIB made some progress. But it never fully dictated terms to industry. When the war ended, the board was shut down right away. Still, its creation pointed toward the government controls that would become necessary in World War II.

## Paying for the War

Most national governments struggled to finance the war. Taxation covered less than one-third of the cost. The rest came from other sources:

- Selling war bonds to the public
- Printing more money
- Taking on additional debt

These choices caused price inflation to hit new highs. Debt, extra money in circulation, and product shortages all squeezed civilian budgets at once.

## Recruiting Soldiers

The British army needed more troops. It launched active recruitment campaigns. One popular tactic was the "pals" unit.

Young men signed up together as a group. They were guaranteed to serve in the same unit. This made enlistment feel like a shared adventure among friends.

But there was a dark side. A whole neighborhood or village could lose nearly all its young men in one battle. The practice ended after the Somme campaign in 1916, which caused very high casualties.

## Russia's Industrial Shortcomings

The war exposed how far behind Russia still was in industrializing. Its railroads were not enough. They could not move troops to the front and food to the cities at the same time. Factory workers went hungry.

Arms manufacturers fell short too. They could not make enough guns or bullets for the soldiers.

This lack of equipment hurt troop morale badly. Soldiers felt their government did not support them. They began to question its decisions.

## 1. Adapting to a Long War

The war was long.

It touched every part of life.

Every country had to change how it worked at home.

 

In Britain and France, many young men joined the army.

Some volunteered.

Others were forced to serve through conscription.

This meant skilled workers left their factories.

Factories needed new workers.

Training those workers took time.

Production slowed down.

 

Germany faced a different problem.

The Allied blockade cut off its raw materials.

Germany had to find new sources.

It could not rely on the old supply routes.

 

## 2. Shells and Politics

Production problems became political problems.

In 1915, British commanders made an accusation.

They said they were turned back in an attack.

The reason was a lack of artillery shells.

This was called the "shell crisis."

 

It raised a hard question.

Who was to blame?

Had the government not ordered enough shells?

Or had the workers not worked hard enough?

 

The British government blamed the army.

It said the military had not placed large enough orders.

Shell output then rose in 1915.

This happened in Britain and in every other combatant nation.

 

## 3. Pressure on the British Government

The British government faced heavy pressure during the war.

The Liberal Party was in power.

But this party had always been against war.

World War One threw the party into confusion.

 

The shell crisis hurt the government's image.

So did the failures at Gallipoli.

Both made the government look weak.

 

David Lloyd George added to the tension.

He served as Minister of Munitions.

He was also a Liberal.

He kept maneuvering against the Prime Minister.

These divisions grew until the end of the war.

 

## 4. The United States and War Production

The United States entered the war later.

Its government moved to control industry in a new way.

It created the War Industries Board.

Barnard Baruch, a financier, ran the board.

The board controlled prices.

It organized production to support the war effort.

 

But the United States had never used central planning before.

It had no experience with centralized economic control.

So it could not command war production the way Britain could.

 

The War Industries Board made some progress.

But it never fully dictated terms to industry.

When the war ended, the board was shut down right away.

Still, its creation pointed toward the government controls that would become necessary in World War Two.

 

## 5. Paying for the War

Most national governments struggled to finance the war.

Taxation covered less than one-third of the cost.

The rest came from other sources:

- Selling war bonds to the public
- Printing more money
- Taking on additional debt

 

These choices caused price inflation to hit new highs.

Debt, extra money in circulation, and product shortages all squeezed civilian budgets at once.

The British army needed more troops.

It launched active recruitment campaigns.

One popular tactic was the "pals" unit.
